title: PackScan: Building real-time sort center analytics with AWS Services
key_points: Amazon's middle-mile team streams every package scan (SNS to Lambda to Firehose) into OpenSearch, and Grafana dashboards refresh every few seconds for sort-centre supervisors.
AWS reports latency going from about an hour to under a minute and a monthly bill dominated by the OpenSearch cluster (about USD 28,000 of roughly USD 35,000).
Useful mainly as a cost reference for second-level operational dashboards.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon Data Firehose, AWS Lambda, Amazon SNS, Grafana
aws_type: Customer Solutions / Experience-Based Acceleration / Technical How-to · (no level)
decision: Search engine vs warehouse vs time-series store as the backend for live operational dashboards
authors: Amazon (Middle Mile) — Sairam Vangapally, Nitin Goyal

title: How Airties achieved scalability and cost-efficiency by moving from Kafka to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
key_points: Airties replaced dozens of fixed-size, single-AZ Kafka clusters with Kinesis streams that scale per stream, ending manual broker and partition work.

They also stopped using long-retention Kafka topics as a lookup store: consumers batch records into bulk files on S3, a DynamoDB index maps device and time to file and offset, and S3 range reads fetch single records.
AWS reports a 33% drop in monthly infrastructure cost and 40% less energy use.
services: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Data Firehose, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, Amazon EMR
decision: Self-managed Kafka vs Kinesis Data Streams for device telemetry; stream retention vs S3 bulk files plus a DynamoDB index for historical lookups
authors: Airties — Steven Aerts, Reza Radmehr, Ramazan Ginkaya

title: Unlock self-serve streaming SQL with Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
key_points: Riskified outgrew ksqlDB for self-service streaming SQL: schema changes meant dropping and recreating streams, its schema-registry conventions clashed with theirs, and jobs competed for shared cluster resources.
Moved to Flink SQL on the managed service, where each job is isolated, a pipeline is one unit, and SQL is validated in CI without a Flink runtime.
Engineers submit SQL through an internal portal that calls the service API; covers an Avro type-mapping limitation and the CI/CD flow.
services: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, Apache Flink SQL, Apache Kafka, Confluent Schema Registry
aws_type: Customer Solutions / Experience-Based Acceleration / Technical How-to · (no level)
decision: ksqlDB vs Flink SQL for self-service streaming SQL on Kafka
authors: Riskified — Gal Krispel, Lorenzo Nicora, Sofie Zilberman

title: Unify streaming and analytical data with Amazon Data Firehose and Amazon SageMaker Lakehouse
key_points: Console walkthrough: create an Iceberg table, point a Firehose stream at it, generate test events and query the table in SageMaker Unified Studio.
Basic; the Nov 2026 streaming-into-Iceberg comparison covers Firehose alongside the other options.
services: Amazon Data Firehose, Apache Iceberg, Amazon SageMaker Lakehouse, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
authors: Kalyan Janaki, Maria Ho, Phaneendra Vuliyaragoli

Feature list for OpenSearch dashboard users.

title: Scalable analytics and centralized governance for Apache Iceberg tables using Amazon S3 Tables and Amazon Redshift
key_points: Loads data into S3 Tables with Spark on EMR, then grants different users table- and column-level access in Lake Formation and shows what each sees from Redshift.
Ends with a single Redshift query joining an S3 Tables table with a local Redshift table.
Read-side only; later posts add Redshift writes to Iceberg.
services: Amazon Redshift, Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, AWS Lake Formation, Amazon EMR
decision: Keep data in Redshift managed storage vs in S3 Tables governed by Lake Formation and queried from Redshift
authors: Satesh Sonti, Jonathan Katz

title: Empower financial analytics by creating structured knowledge bases using Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Redshift
key_points: Bedrock Knowledge Bases can point at a Redshift database and turn plain-English questions into SQL, run it, and answer in prose; the generated SQL can be inspected.
Set-up is a database user for the Bedrock service role with SELECT on chosen tables, then a sync; accuracy improves by limiting tables and supplying curated example queries.
Security advice: read-only roles and one knowledge base per team's table scope.
services: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, Amazon Redshift Serverless, Amazon Nova
decision: Managed text-to-SQL (Bedrock Knowledge Bases) vs custom agent with MCP tools vs BI-tool Q&A for natural-language questions on the warehouse
attaches_to: dbt-pipelines (NYC 311 on Redshift Serverless as the test set); aws-bytes: GenAI on data (later)
authors: Nita Shah, Jonathan Katz, Sushmita Barthakur

title: Simplify enterprise data access using the Amazon Redshift integration with Amazon S3 Access Grants
key_points: With S3 Access Grants, Redshift's COPY and UNLOAD run with the signed-in Identity Center user's S3 permissions instead of one IAM role attached to the warehouse.
Grants are given to directory groups for a bucket or prefix, so access changes by group membership rather than policy edits; the example works across accounts.
Useful for multi-team warehouses where who can load or export which S3 path must be auditable per person.
services: Amazon Redshift, Amazon S3 Access Grants, AWS IAM Identity Center
decision: Shared warehouse IAM role vs per-user S3 Access Grants for Redshift COPY/UNLOAD
attaches_to: aws-bytes: governance (later); S3 cross-account migration (done) follow-up
authors: Maneesh Sharma, Praveen Kumar Ramakrishnan, Laura Reith, Yanzhu Ji

title: How LaunchDarkly migrated to Amazon MWAA to achieve efficiency and scale
key_points: LaunchDarkly's planned lift-and-shift to MWAA broke because a custom operator relied on the old platform's Kubernetes executor isolation; tasks clashed on MWAA's shared Celery workers.
Fix: each task runs as its own ECS Fargate task started from Airflow, through a thin wrapper so analysts just give a command.
AWS reports growth from about 100 to over 14,000 tasks a day with little added cost, and a reusable Terraform module for new environments.
services: Amazon MWAA, Amazon ECS, AWS Fargate, Apache Airflow
decision: Run task code inside Airflow workers vs isolated containers (ECS Fargate vs EKS pods)
authors: LaunchDarkly — Asena Uyar, Dean Verhey, Daniel Lopes

title: Access Amazon Redshift Managed Storage tables through Apache Spark on AWS Glue and Amazon EMR using Amazon SageMaker Lakehouse
key_points: Tables in Redshift managed storage can be read and written by Spark on Glue 5.0 or EMR through the Iceberg REST catalog, using one copy of the data.
Walkthrough sets up a Lakehouse catalog for the managed storage, then runs the Spark code from Unified Studio notebooks, Glue and EMR Serverless.
Lets Spark jobs work on warehouse tables without UNLOAD/COPY round trips.
services: Amazon Redshift, AWS Glue, Amazon EMR, Amazon SageMaker Lakehouse, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Apache Iceberg
decision: UNLOAD to S3 for Spark vs Spark reading Redshift managed storage through the Iceberg REST catalog
authors: Noritaka Sekiyama, Angel Conde Manjon, Raj Ramasubbu, Stefano Sandona, Derek Liu

title: Zero-copy, Coordination-free approach to OpenSearch Snapshots

Internal engine improvement, nothing for the reader to apply.

title: Petabyte-scale data migration made simple: AppsFlyer’s best practice journey with Amazon EMR Serverless
key_points: AppsFlyer moved Spark work off about 100 self-managed Hadoop clusters to EMR Serverless; AWS reports roughly 100 PB processed a day.
A central infra team prepared templates, an Airflow operator, cross-account roles and a support channel so product teams could migrate themselves.
Chose plain JARs over custom images (images cost compute time while they download), with GitOps deployment and rollbacks, Spline for lineage and a log-shipping plugin for Datadog.
services: Amazon EMR Serverless, Apache Spark, Apache Airflow, Spline, Datadog
decision: Self-managed Hadoop vs EMR Serverless for many teams' Spark jobs; custom images vs JAR deployment
authors: AppsFlyer — Roy Ninio, Avichay Marciano, Eitav Arditti, Yonatan Dolan

title: Configure cross-account access of Amazon SageMaker Lakehouse multi-catalog tables using AWS Glue 5.0 Spark
key_points: A producer account shares both a Redshift table and an S3 Iceberg table through Lake Formation; the consumer account joins them in one Glue 5.0 Spark job without copying either.
Extends to a data mesh with a central governance account, and to other Regions through resource links.
Consumer side needs a catalog link container plus table and database resource links before granting the Glue job role access; Athena is used to check access first.
services: AWS Glue, AWS Lake Formation, Amazon SageMaker Lakehouse, Amazon Redshift, Apache Iceberg
decision: Copy warehouse data to the lake for other accounts vs share Redshift and lake tables in place through Lake Formation
authors: Aarthi Srinivasan, Subhasis Sarkar

title: Accelerate lightweight analytics using PyIceberg with AWS Lambda and an AWS Glue Iceberg REST endpoint
key_points: PyIceberg lets plain Python (no Spark) create, append to and time-travel Iceberg tables through the Glue Iceberg REST endpoint, so a Lambda can be the writer.
Example loads NYC yellow-taxi records from a container-image Lambda, explores snapshots and tags from a notebook with pandas, then queries the same table in Athena.
Single-node limits apply, and concurrent Lambda invocations can clash on commits, so retries and capped concurrency are needed.
services: AWS Lambda, Apache Iceberg, PyIceberg, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Amazon Athena, Amazon S3
decision: PyIceberg in Lambda vs Glue Spark vs DuckDB for small, event-driven writes to Iceberg tables

title: Save big on OpenSearch: Unleashing Intel AVX-512 for binary vector performance
key_points: OpenSearch 2.19 uses newer Intel CPU instructions to speed up distance calculations on binary (1-bit) vectors when data nodes run on the latest Intel instance families.

title: Automate replication of row-level security from AWS Lake Formation to AWS Quick Sight
key_points: Identity propagation keeps row filters at the source, but it needs Identity Center and rules out SPICE; this post copies Lake Formation row filters into Quick Sight's own row-level security instead.
A Lambda reads the data filters and grants, rewrites them as Quick Sight rules files in S3, and a rules dataset applies them to dashboards.
Must be re-run on a schedule or on permission-change events, otherwise the two places drift apart.
services: AWS Lake Formation, Amazon Quick Sight, AWS Lambda, Amazon S3
decision: Enforce row security at the source with identity propagation vs replicate rules into the BI tool (to keep SPICE)
authors: Vetri Natarajan, Ismael Murillo
